questions.question_text: Find the stationary points of $y=(x-4)^{2}(x+2)$ and their nature.

options.text: A maximum at $(0,32)$ and a minimum at $(4,0)$
A minimum at $(0,32)$ and a maximum at $(4,0)$
options.why: Swapped the natures; $P''(0)=-12<0$ makes $(0,32)$ a maximum and $P''(4)=12>0$ makes $(4,0)$ a minimum.

options.text: A maximum at $(0,-32)$ and a minimum at $(4,0)$
options.why: Sign slip evaluating the $y$-value: $P(0)=(0-4)^{2}(0+2)=16\times2=32$, not $-32$.

options.text: A minimum at $(0,-32)$ and a maximum at $(4,0)$
options.why: Both slips together: the sign error in $P(0)$ and the swapped natures.

questions.solution_text:
$P(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+32$
$P'(x)=3x^{2}-12x$
$=3x(x-4)$
$x=0$ or $x=4$
$P(0)=32$
$P(4)=0$
$P''(x)=6x-12$
$P''(0)=-12<0$, so $(0,32)$ is a maximum.
$P''(4)=12>0$, so $(4,0)$ is a minimum.

\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$}, xmin=-2.7, xmax=6.8, ymin=-12.5, ymax=45.5, samples=120, clip=false, width=9cm, height=8cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, <->, domain=-2.3:6.33] {(x-4)*(x-4)*(x+2)};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

questions.question_text:
The graph of $y=x(x+2)^{2}$ has a stationary point that lies on the $x$-axis.
Where is it?

options.why: $x=0$ is a simple zero, so the curve cuts the axis there and is not stationary.
Sign error: the factor $(x+2)^{2}$ gives the repeated zero $x=-2$.
This is the other stationary point, but it is below the axis, not on it.

questions.solution_text:
$P(x)=x^{3}+4x^{2}+4x$
$P'(x)=3x^{2}+8x+4$
$=(3x+2)(x+2)$
$x=-2$ or $x=-\dfrac{2}{3}$
$P(-2)=0$
$P\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)=-\dfrac{32}{27}$
Only $x=-2$ gives $y=0$, and it is the double zero, so the stationary point on the axis is $(-2,0)$.

\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$}, xmin=-3.6, xmax=1.2, ymin=-4.5, ymax=6.5, samples=120, clip=false, width=9cm, height=8cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, <->, domain=-3.13:0.78] {x*(x+2)*(x+2)};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

questions.question_text: Which statement about the graph of $y=(x-1)^{2}(x+3)^{2}$ is correct?

options.text: It touches the $x$-axis at $(1,0)$ and $(-3,0)$, with a maximum at $(-1,16)$.
It touches the $x$-axis at $(1,0)$ and $(-3,0)$, with a maximum at $(-1,4)$.
options.why: Evaluated only one bracket at $x=-1$; the full value is $P(-1)=(-2)^{2}(2)^{2}=4\times4=16$, not $4$.

options.text: It cuts the $x$-axis at $(1,0)$ and $(-3,0)$, with a maximum at $(-1,16)$.
options.why: Read each zero as multiplicity $1$; both zeroes have multiplicity $2$, so the curve touches the axis and turns back rather than crossing.

options.text: It cuts the $x$-axis at $(1,0)$ and $(-3,0)$, with a maximum at $(-1,4)$.
options.why: Both slips together: the zeroes read as simple, and only one bracket evaluated at $x=-1$.

questions.solution_text:
$P(x)=\left(x^{2}+2x-3\right)^{2}$
$P'(x)=2\left(x^{2}+2x-3\right)(2x+2)$
$x=1$, $x=-3$ or $x=-1$
$P(1)=0$
$P(-3)=0$
$P(-1)=(-2)^{2}(2)^{2}$
$=4\times4$
$=16$
Both zeroes have multiplicity $2$, so they are minimums on the axis, and $(-1,16)$ between them is a maximum.

\addplot[smooth, thick, <->, domain=-3.95:1.95] {(x-1)*(x-1)*(x+3)*(x+3)};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

questions.question_text: Describe the behaviour of $y=-2(x+1)^{3}(x-3)$ as $x\to\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty$.

options.why: The degree is even, so both ends do agree, but the leading coefficient $-2$ makes them both negative.
Opposite ends require an odd degree; here the degree is $4$.
Opposite ends require an odd degree, and the degree here is $4$.

questions.question_text: How many stationary points does $y=(x-2)^{3}(x+2)$ have, and how many of them lie on the $x$-axis?

options.text: $2$ stationary points, $1$ of them on the $x$-axis

options.why: The triple zero $x=2$ is itself a stationary point, and it lies on the axis.

options.text: $3$ stationary points, $1$ of them on the $x$-axis
options.why: Counted the repeated factor $(x-2)^{2}$ in $P'$ as two separate stationary points.
Missed the factor $4x+4$ in $P'$, which gives a second stationary point at $x=-1$.

questions.solution_text:
$P'(x)=3(x-2)^{2}(x+2)+(x-2)^{3}$
$=(x-2)^{2}(3x+6+x-2)$
$=(x-2)^{2}(4x+4)$
$x=2$ or $x=-1$
$P(2)=0$
$P(-1)=(-3)^{3}(1)$
$=-27$
So there are $2$ stationary points, and only $(2,0)$ lies on the $x$-axis.

\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$}, xmin=-2.9, xmax=4.3, ymin=-40.5, ymax=40.5, samples=120, clip=false, width=9cm, height=8cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, <->, domain=-2.45:3.89] {(x-2)*(x-2)*(x-2)*(x+2)};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

questions.question_text: How many times does the graph of $y=x^{2}(x+4)^{2}$ cross the $x$-axis?

options.why: Counted the two $x$-intercepts, but at each one the multiplicity is even so the curve touches instead of crossing.
Assumed an even-degree curve must cross once; both zeroes are turning points on the axis.
Counted the degree, which is the number of zeroes with multiplicity, not the number of crossings.

questions.question_text:
A cubic curve touches the $x$-axis at $x=-3$, cuts it at $x=2$, and has $y$-intercept $-18$.
What is its equation, and what is the nature of the stationary point at $x=-3$?

options.why: The curve rises to the axis and falls away again to the right, so $(-3,0)$ is a maximum; $P''(-3)=-10<0$.
The signs inside the brackets are reversed, giving intercepts at $3$ and $-2$.
Sign error in $k$: $y=k(9)(-2)=-18k=-18$ gives $k=1$, not $-1$.

questions.solution_text:
Touching at $x=-3$ needs an even multiplicity, so $(x+3)^{2}$ is a factor.
$y=k(x+3)^{2}(x-2)$
$-18=k(3)^{2}(-2)$
$-18=-18k$
$k=1$
$y=(x+3)^{2}(x-2)$
$P(x)=x^{3}+4x^{2}-3x-18$
$P''(x)=6x+8$
$P''(-3)=-10<0$, so $(-3,0)$ is a maximum.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$}, xmin=-5.3, xmax=3.2, ymin=-25.5, ymax=25.5, samples=120, clip=false, width=9cm, height=8cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, <->, domain=-4.9:2.76] {(x+3)*(x+3)*(x-2)};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
